newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Wary U.N. prepares to vote on Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: Wary U.N. prepares to vote on Zaire mission.

text.p: U.N. Security Council members hoped to vote on Friday on a resolution to send a multinational force to ease the plight of an estimated one million starving refugees in war-ravaged eastern Zaire.

The international community signalled it was wary of the hazards ahead as fighting erupted on Thursday around the teeming Mugunga refugee camp near the rebel-held Zairean town of Goma on the border with Rwanda. Armed Hutus among the refugees were putting up a last stand against the Tutsi rebels.
The United States said it would demand at least an informal ceasefire among the factions fighting around Goma before committing troops to a humanitarian aid force in Zaire.

"What we would like is a pledge by the sides that there will be a ceasefire," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters. But he said that such a "defacto ceasefire" between warring Hutu and Tutsi militia groups would not have to be "a written, signed agreement".

At the United Nations in New York, the Canadian commander of the force intended to deliver humanitarian aid to eastern Zaire ruled out disarming militia mingling in the refugee camps or separating them from civilians.
Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril told a news conference his troops, estimated to eventually exceed 10,000, would not use force unless they were attacked.
U.N. officials said earlier that feeding areas would be set up by the troops and that no armed militia would be allowed to enter. But Baril made no mention of this.

Although the force is not being organised by the United Nations, all participating countries want the Security Council's seal of approval for the mission. The draft resolution would authorise it under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter which allows the use of force.
The resolution, subject to change, says the mission would terminate no later than March 31 after which another operation would take its place.
Diplomats said this so-called "follow-on" force would probably be run by the United Nations and include some of the troops expected to go to eastern Zaire shortly.
In the meantime, the costs of the multinational force would be borne by those countries taking part.
The resolution, obtained by Reuters, urges contributions for a fund set up by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to help any African nations who want to participate.
Diplomats said the initial force was expected to be made up of troops from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.
Other countries expected to join at a later date were Cameroon, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt, Mali, Ireland, Brazil and Portugal. Norway and Finland might send human rights observers.

President Bill Clinton tentatively pledged on Wednesday to send about 1,000 U.S. troops to Goma and about 3,000 to nearby countries as part of a task force to save more than one million refugees if details could be worked out.
The United States, still smarting from losses in a peacekeeping mission in Somalia four years ago, and Britain have moved cautiously by sending assessment teams to the region.

Troop-contributing nations and other delegations held a series of meetings with Baril in New York in an effort to define the force's mandate. Baril said he intended to establish his headquarters for the intervention force in Goma.

France, which has led calls for an international mission to help the some 1.2 million mainly Hutu refugees uprooted by fighting between Zaire and Tutsi rebels, has said it is ready to send between 1,500 and 2,000 soldiers. They would include 600 paratroopers able to go within 24 hours of U.N. approval.
France seemed to be opting for a high-risk deployment of its planned contingent in Zaire that could put it in the midst of Tutsi rebels openly distrustful of the French.

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said France would "contribute to ensuring the safety of the platform at Bukavu". Rebel-held Bukavu has one of the main airports in eastern Zaire which would be a key staging post for the mission.
Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsis battling the Zairean army and Hutu militias accuse France of backing Hutus who massacred Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994 and then fled en masse to Zaire.
They say a French military intervention in Rwanda that year aided the escape of armed Hutu genocide leaders who are now battling the Tutsi rebels using refugees as a screen.
Some Tutsi spokesmen have openly vowed to fight the French. France denies charges of bias in the Hutu-Tutsi conflict.
